steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on distributed influence-augmented local simulators for parallel multi-agent RL in large networked systems. Use traffic light control in a big city as the running example, explain why local simulators need influence modelling, what goes wrong when many agents learn at once, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivating example: training traffic-light agents for a very large city
2. Local simulators, coupling between regions, and influence-based abstraction
3. Extending IBA to multiple agents and the non-stationarity caveat
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Traffic example
- city too large for a single policy -> split into sub-regions, one traffic light per agent
- local observations only: partial observability may affect optimal policies but makes each decision problem more manageable
- local rewards: reduce variance of returns, facilitate credit assignment
- train all together on a big global traffic simulator -> weeks or months if city truly large; assuming training converges

2. Local simulators and IBA
- observations/rewards local -> train on separate local simulators (cars moving within each sub-region)
- works if local transitions isolated from rest of system; breaks when regions coupled (regions part of larger system, depend on one another)
- solution: model influence of global system on each local region; not the entire system (else just use global simulator)
- traffic: many external variables affect a region (e.g. traffic densities elsewhere), only a small subset directly (e.g. road segments connecting intersections to rest of city) = influence sources
- Influence-Based Abstraction: posterior of influence sources given action local state history (ALSH) -> realistic trajectories matching global simulator
- influence-augmented local simulator (IALS): effective in single agent scenarios with planning and RL algorithms

3. Multi-agent extension
- extend IBA to multi-agent domains; factorize large networked systems into sub-regions; replace GS by distributed network of IALSs running independently, in parallel
- caveat: IBA assumes single learning agent -> stationary influence distributions
- simultaneous learning -> old influence distributions invalid after policy updates
- naive fix: recompute every time any agent updates; impractical (costs) and undesirable
- Section 4.1: multiple (similar) joint policies may induce same influence distributions; small variations can elicit same optimal policies
- Section 4.3: keeping previous influence distributions -> local transitions biased but stationary; possibly an advantage

4. Contributions
- (1) adapt IBA to MARL; simultaneous learning without major computational costs
- (2) distribute simulation among processes -> parallel training, scale to many agents
- (3) non-stationarity issues of MARL partly mitigated by this training scheme

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Imagine that we have to train a team of agents to control the traffic lights of a very large city, so large that we can't control all the traffic lights with a single policy. The first step would be splitting the problem into multiple sub-regions, and a natural way to divide it is to assign one traffic light to each agent. Then, because the agents act locally, we would limit their observations to only local information. This partial observability could affect their optimal policies, but it would also make each individual decision-making problem more manageable. We may also want to reward the agents only for what happens in their local neighborhood, so that the variance of the returns is reduced and credit assignment is easier. Finally, we could train all the agents together on a big traffic simulator that reproduces the global dynamics. But if the city is really large, optimizing their policies could take weeks or even months. And that is assuming that training actually converges.

One could argue that since the observations and rewards of the agents are local, we could just as well train them on separate simulators that only model the local transition dynamics (i.e. cars moving within each of the sub-regions). This might work if the local transitions of the agents are isolated from the rest of the system, but it would probably break when the local regions are coupled. The reason is that the local simulators would not account for the fact that the local regions of the agents are part of a larger system and depend on each other. One solution is to model the influence that the global system exerts on each local region. Luckily, this does not necessarily mean modelling the whole system, otherwise we would just use the global simulator. In many scenarios, like the traffic problem, the local regions may be affected by many external variables (e.g. traffic densities in other parts of the city), but they are only directly influenced by a small subset of them (e.g. road segments that connect the intersections with the rest of the city). This subset of variables is called the influence sources. The theoretical framework of Influence-Based Abstraction shows that if one monitors the posterior distribution of the influence sources given the action local state history (ALSH), one can simulate realistic trajectories that match the ones produced by the global simulator. The resulting simulator is known as the influence-augmented local simulator (IALS), and it has been proven effective in single agent scenarios when it is combined with planning and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms.

3. Multi-agent extension
- extend IBA to multi-agent domains; factorize large networked systems into sub-regions; replace GS by distributed network of IALSs running independently, in parallel
- caveat: IBA assumes single learning agent -> stationary influence distributions
- simultaneous learning -> old influence distributions invalid after policy updates
- naive fix: recompute every time any agent updates; impractical (costs) and undesirable
- Section 4.1: multiple (similar) joint policies may induce same influence distributions; small variations can elicit same optimal policies
- Section 4.3: keeping previous influence distributions -> local transitions biased but stationary; possibly an advantage

4. Contributions
- (1) adapt IBA to MARL; simultaneous learning without major computational costs
- (2) distribute simulation among processes -> parallel training, scale to many agents
- (3) non-stationarity issues of MARL partly mitigated by this training scheme

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Imagine that we have to train a team of agents to control the traffic lights of a very large city, so large that we can't control all the traffic lights with a single policy. The first step would be splitting the problem into multiple sub-regions, and a natural way to divide it is to assign one traffic light to each agent. Then, because the agents act locally, we would limit their observations to only local information. This partial observability could affect their optimal policies, but it would also make each individual decision-making problem more manageable. We may also want to reward the agents only for what happens in their local neighborhood, so that the variance of the returns is reduced and credit assignment is easier. Finally, we could train all the agents together on a big traffic simulator that reproduces the global dynamics. But if the city is really large, optimizing their policies could take weeks or even months. And that is assuming that training actually converges.

One could argue that since the observations and rewards of the agents are local, we could just as well train them on separate simulators that only model the local transition dynamics (i.e. cars moving within each of the sub-regions). This might work if the local transitions of the agents are isolated from the rest of the system, but it would probably break when the local regions are coupled. The reason is that the local simulators would not account for the fact that the local regions of the agents are part of a larger system and depend on each other. One solution is to model the influence that the global system exerts on each local region. Luckily, this does not necessarily mean modelling the whole system, otherwise we would just use the global simulator. In many scenarios, like the traffic problem, the local regions may be affected by many external variables (e.g. traffic densities in other parts of the city), but they are only directly influenced by a small subset of them (e.g. road segments that connect the intersections with the rest of the city). This subset of variables is called the influence sources. The theoretical framework of Influence-Based Abstraction shows that if one monitors the posterior distribution of the influence sources given the action local state history (ALSH), one can simulate realistic trajectories that match the ones produced by the global simulator. The resulting simulator is known as the influence-augmented local simulator (IALS), and it has been proven effective in single agent scenarios when it is combined with planning and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms.

In this paper we extend the IBA framework to multi-agent domains. We show how large networked systems like the traffic example above can be factorized into multiple sub-regions so that the GS can be replaced by a distributed network of IALSs that run independently and in parallel. There is one important caveat. The IBA framework assumes that only a single agent is learning at a time. This assumption is needed so that the influence distributions are stationary. In our case, since we want the agents to learn at the same time, this means that influence distributions computed before would not be valid anymore after the agents update their policies. The naive solution would be to compute new influence distributions every time any agent updates its policy. But we argue that this is not only impractical, because recomputing the distributions has costs, but also undesirable. The theoretical results in Section 4.1 show that multiple (similar) joint policies may induce the same influence distributions, and that even when they vary a little they can still lead to the same optimal policies. Also, our insights in Section 4.3 suggest that what looks like a problem at first may actually be an advantage, since in many situations keeping the previous influence distributions means that the local transitions stay stationary, although they are biased.

The main contributions of this paper are: (1) we adapt IBA to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and show that simultaneous learning is possible without major computational costs, (2) we show that by distributing the simulation among different processes we can parallelize training and scale up to systems with many agents, (3) we show that the non-stationarity issues that are inherent to MARL are partly mitigated as a result of this training scheme.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Imagine we have to train a team of agents to control the traffic lights of a very large city, so large that we simply cannot control all traffic lights with a single policy. The first step would be to split the problem into multiple sub-regions. A natural division would be to assign one traffic light to each agent. Then, since the agents act locally, we would limit their observations to local information only. This partial observability could affect their optimal policies, but it would also make each individual decision-making problem more manageable [1,2]. We may also want to reward agents only for what occurs in their local neighborhood, so that we reduce the variance of the returns [3] and facilitate credit assignment [4]. Finally, we could train all agents together on a big traffic simulator that reproduces the global dynamics. However, if the city is truly large, optimizing their policies could take weeks or even months. That is assuming training converges at all.

One may argue that, since the agents' observations and rewards are local, we could just as well train them on separate simulators that model only the local transition dynamics (i.e. cars moving within each of the sub-regions; [5]). This approach might work if the agents' local transitions are isolated from the rest of the system [6], but would probably break when the local regions are coupled, because the local simulators would fail to account for the fact that the agents' local regions belong to a larger system and depend on one another. A solution is to model the influence the global system exerts on each local region. Fortunately, this does not necessarily mean modelling the entire system, or else we would just use the global simulator. In many scenarios, such as the traffic problem, the local regions may be affected by many external variables (e.g., traffic densities in other parts of the city), but they are only directly influenced by a small subset of them (e.g., road segments that connect the intersections with the rest of the city). This subset of variables is known as the influence sources. The theoretical framework of Influence-Based Abstraction [7] shows that by monitoring the posterior distribution of the influence sources given the action local state history (ALSH), one can simulate realistic trajectories that match those produced by the global simulator. The resulting simulator, known as the influence-augmented local simulator (IALS), has been proven effective in single agent scenarios when combined with planning [8] and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms [9].

In this paper, we extend the IBA framework to multi-agent domains. We show how to factorize large networked systems, such as the traffic example above, into multiple sub-regions so that the GS can be replaced by a distributed network of IALSs that run independently and in parallel. There is one important caveat. The IBA framework assumes that only a single agent is learning at a time, which is needed to keep the influence distributions stationary. In our case, since we want the agents to learn simultaneously, this implies that previously computed influence distributions would no longer be valid once the agents update their policies. The naive solution would be to recompute the influence distributions every time any agent updates its policy. However, we argue that this is not only impractical, since recomputing the distributions has a cost, but also undesirable. The theoretical results in Section 4.1 demonstrate that multiple (similar) joint policies may induce the same influence distributions, and that even when these vary a little, they can still elicit the same optimal policies. Further, our insights in Section 4.3 hint that what seems to be a problem at first may in fact be an advantage, since in many situations maintaining the previous influence distributions means that the local transitions, although biased, remain stationary.

The main contributions of this paper are: (1) adapting IBA to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and demonstrating that simultaneous learning is possible without major computational costs, (2) showing that by distributing the simulation among different processes we can parallelize training and scale up to systems with many agents, (3) revealing that the non-stationarity issues inherent to MARL are partly mitigated by this training scheme.
